issues.legal_issue: A uniform income-capitalization method for valuing acquired land in municipal areas, distinct from the valuation method for rural land, does not deny equal protection merely because owners of municipal land cannot use every valuation method available under the general land-acquisition regime.
material_facts: The challenged provisions applied one valuation method to land in municipal areas, while a different method applied to rural land.

The municipal-area method calculated the acquisition amount by reference to income derived from the land, including a prescribed deduction for expenses and a method for valuing land that had been vacant or unrented.
The distinction applied uniformly to all land in each category, and municipal land had greater potentialities than rural land.
Capitalization was a recognized method of valuation, and the Court found no adequate material establishing hostile discrimination or that the resulting amount was illusory.
issues.conclusion: The challenged valuation provisions did not violate Article 14 of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: Legislation is presumed constitutional, and a challenger must provide adequate material to displace that presumption. Article 14 does not require that every recognized method of determining market value be available in every land category. The Court relied on State of Gujarat v. Shri Shantilal Mangaldas, Prakash Amichand Shah v. State of Gujarat, Raja Vyricherla Narayana Gajapatiraju v. Revenue Divisional Officer, Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India, Union of India v. Shanti Devi, Special Land Acquisition Officer, Davangere v. P. Veerabhadrappa, and Oriental Gas Co. Ltd. v. State of West Bengal.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A party challenges the constitutionality of provisions governing valuation of land acquired by the state.
predicates.municipal_land_is_valued_by_a_uniform_in: The same income-based valuation method is applied to all acquired land in municipal areas.
predicates.municipal_and_rural_land_have_different_: The land in municipal areas has potentialities different from those of land in rural areas.
predicates.capitalization_is_a_recognized_valuation: The method used to value the acquired land is a recognized method of property valuation.
predicates.challenger_lacks_adequate_evidence_of_ho: The challenger does not provide adequate material showing that the valuation scheme discriminates hostilely against the affected landowners.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a uniform income-based valuation method for municipal land, and the land categories differ in potentialities, the method is recognized, and adequate evidence of hostile discrimination is lacking, the distinct method does not violate equal protection.

issues.legal_issue: A law whose contents provide for acquisition and distribution of land and related amenities for community housing can be protected as implementing the constitutional policy of distributing material resources for the common good, without an express legislative declaration of that purpose.
material_facts: The legislation provided for acquiring private land, developing it, and making housing sites or accommodation available to the community.
It also provided for land and facilities such as community centres, shopping complexes, parks, roads, drains, and playgrounds that serve residents collectively.
The legislation's contents, rather than an express declaration of its purpose, showed its relationship to distribution of material resources.
issues.conclusion: The legislation implemented the policy in Article 39(b) and was protected by Article 31C against a challenge based on Articles 14 and 19, even assuming an infringement of Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31C applies according to the character and contents of legislation; it does not require an express legislative declaration. Article 39(b)'s reference to distribution of material resources is construed broadly enough to include the acquisition, development, and distribution of land and community amenities. The Court relied on His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalavaru v. State of Kerala, Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India, State of Karnataka v. Shri Ranganatha Reddy, and Sanjeev Coke Manufacturing Company v. Bharat Coking Coal Ltd.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_a_housing_an: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law providing for land acquisition and housing or related development.
predicates.law_provides_for_acquiring_and_developin: The law provides for private land to be acquired and developed for public use.
predicates.developed_land_and_shared_amenities_are_: The law provides for housing sites or accommodation and shared civic facilities to serve the community.

issues.definition: If a challenged housing and land-distribution law acquires and develops private land for community housing and shared amenities, it is protected from equal-protection and freedom challenges as implementing distribution for the common good.

issues.legal_issue: Acquisition of property under a public housing law does not infringe the constitutional protection against deprivation of property where the acquisition serves a public purpose, owners can make representations, and the acquisition amount is determined by a method regarded as fair.
material_facts: The acquired property consisted of vacant land in a municipal area intended to provide housing accommodation.
The owners had an opportunity to make representations before the acquisition notification was issued.
The acquisition amount was calculated under a valuation method the Court regarded as fair.

The proceedings began after the property-protection guarantee in Article 300A came into force, while the Court noted that Article 31(1), in materially similar language, had been in force when the legislation was enacted; the Court assumed, without deciding, that Article 300A applied.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition provisions did not infringe Article 300A; the Court also held that the acquisition satisfied the requirements of a valid exercise of eminent domain.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assumed without deciding that Article 300A applied to the acquisition and that fairness was required, but concluded that the public purpose, opportunity to make representations, and fair valuation method satisfied those requirements. It also held that Article 31C protected the law even if it infringed the then-applicable Article 31.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_acq: A party challenges the constitutionality of a state acquisition of private property.
predicates.property_is_taken_for_public_housing: The state acquires the property to provide housing accommodation for the public.
predicates.owners_can_make_representations_before_a: The affected owners are given an opportunity to present their objections before the acquisition is finalized.
predicates.acquisition_amount_uses_a_fair_valuation: The acquisition amount is determined by a valuation method regarded as fair.

issues.definition: When a property acquisition is for public housing, owners can object before it is finalized, and the amount is determined by a fair valuation method, the acquisition does not infringe the property-protection guarantee.

issues.legal_issue: Article 21 does not invalidate land-acquisition or housing legislation merely because it deprives an owner of property, where the deprivation does not result in loss of life, liberty, or livelihood and the acquisition is intended to improve living conditions for a larger population.
material_facts: The challenged law authorized acquisition of land to provide housing accommodation.
The case did not involve deprivation of property that would lead to deprivation of life, liberty, or livelihood.
The acquisition was intended to improve the living conditions of a larger number of people.
issues.conclusion: Article 21 did not provide a basis for striking down the challenged provisions.
issues.legal_principle: Article 21 essentially concerns personal liberty and does not, by itself, protect the right to own property in the circumstances presented. The Court distinguished property deprivation that would lead to deprivation of life, liberty, or livelihood from acquisition intended to improve conditions for a larger population.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_a_land_acqui: A party invokes the constitutional protection of personal liberty to challenge a land-acquisition or housing law.
predicates.property_deprivation_does_not_deprive_li: The property loss does not also deprive the affected person of life, personal liberty, or livelihood.
predicates.acquisition_improves_living_conditions_f: The property is acquired to improve living conditions for a larger group of people.

issues.definition: If a challenge to a land-acquisition or housing law involves no resulting deprivation of life, liberty, or livelihood and the acquisition improves living conditions for a larger population, the law cannot be invalidated on the personal-liberty ground.

issues.legal_issue: Case-specific difficulty in valuing open land or land with development potential does not establish that a generally applicable valuation provision is unconstitutional.
material_facts: The challengers identified possible difficulties applying the valuation rules to open land and land with building potential in large towns.
The Court treated those difficulties as matters of valuation in individual cases that the authorities could resolve in accordance with law.
issues.conclusion: The identified valuation difficulties did not affect the constitutionality of the challenged provisions.
issues.legal_principle: A practical difficulty in applying a valuation rule to particular land is not, without more, a ground for invalidating the rule itself; the valuation authorities must resolve individual valuation problems in accordance with law.

predicates.facial_challenge_to_a_general_valuation_: A party challenges the validity of a valuation rule that applies generally to acquired land.
predicates.asserted_difficulty_is_limited_to_indivi: The claimed problem concerns how the rule applies to particular land, such as open land or land with development potential.

issues.definition: When a general valuation rule is challenged but the asserted difficulty concerns only valuation of particular land, that difficulty does not invalidate the rule.
